newsitem.title: BELGIUM: BELGIAN INTERBREW SEES HIGHER 1996 PROFITS.
newsitem.headline: BELGIAN INTERBREW SEES HIGHER 1996 PROFITS.

text.p: Belgian brewing giant Interbrew said on Tuesday 1996 results would be better than the previous year's, and that it hoped to make further acquistions in 1997.

"It's not easy to stay profitable in beer. Consumption is going down, certainly in Europe and particularly in Belgium. For the future we must try to do better at a lower cost," Interbrew spokesman Jan Coucke told Reuters.

He confirmed comments made to Belgian newspaper L'Echo by Paul De Keersmaecker, the president of Interbrew's board, and Johnny Thijs, the company's chief executive officer, who said 1996 results would be boosted by Canadian unit Labatt.
Labatt would be fully consolidated for the first time in 1996 results, the Belgian group told L'Echo, which would "necessarily have a positive influence on our results".

Privately-held Interbrew, best known for its Stella Artois brand, made a group net profit of 3.5 billion francs in the 15 months to end December 1995. Total sales - which included five months'-worth from Labatt - were 28.9 million hectolitres.
Interbrew became one of the biggest brewing groups in the world when it acquired John Labatt Co in 1995 in a $2 billion takeover.
De Keersmaecker and Thijs told L'Echo Interbrew would try to make "one or two" acquisitions in 1997, and the company would continue to manage its brands, market share and costs well.
The company repeated past comments that it had no plans to float on the stock market but if a situation arose which needed ad hoc financing a flotation could be envisaged.
